speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the protocol for the revision of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice, signed at Geneva in respect of the Dominion of Canada, on the 14th September, 1929, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: The protocol being submitted for approval of this house was signed for the Dominion of Canada by Senator Dandurand at Geneva on the 14th September, 1929, and is subject to ratification. In the ten years that have elapsed since the creation of the permanent court, the experience of its actual working arrangements has indicated that certain improvements in its organization were necessary. The French delegates were voicing a very general feeling when, at the ninth assembly, they proposed that the statute of the court be examined with a view to the introduction of such amendments as may be judged desirable. In accordance with this resolution which was unanimously adopted, the council appointed a committee of jurists which undertook the work of revision. Their report was submitted by the council of the league to a conference of states, parties to the statute of the permanent court which met at Geneva in September, 1929, for the purpose of examining the amendments of the statute recommended by the committee of jurists. This conference, in which Sir George Foster represented the Dominion of Canada, adopted a draft protocol of amendments which was aproved by the tenth assembly on the 14th September. It is not necessaiy at this point to examine in detail the changes embodied in the protocol whose ratification we have under consideration. They represent, for the most part, modifications in the structure and procedure of the court which its decade of experience has suggested as necessary. Inasmuch as the entire court is to be reelected this year it has seemed desirable that the recommended changes be put into practice as speedily as possible.
The motion is largely of a formal nature and I think I have given the house all the information in regard thereto which will be necessary.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext:
It has not been ratified as yet
by other countries?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE

speechtext:
I agree largely with the
statement of the Prime Minister that this motion is mainly of a formal character. Nevertheless, it involves a responsibility which, if discharged, would do much towards making it impossible to have recourse to war for the settlement of differences 'between nations. I understand that most of the nations concerned have accepted thi3 revised statute dealing with the international court. I notice the next resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister deals with the acceptance of the reservations made by the United States. It will be remembered that Mr. Root is largely responsible for preparing the reservations under which the United States is willing to accept the revised statute with respect to the world court. My memory is not clear as to whether or not the revised statute has been formally accepted with reservations by the United States. The only reason I asked the question was that in the event of its not being accepted it might be that this protocol would be again amended or that a condition would be imposed upon it before the senate of the United States would accept it. I asked the question for the purpose of clearing it up in my own mind.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister tell me if there is a code of laws drawn up for the guidance of the international court of justice? If there is such a document I should like to have a copy of it. If such a code does not exist for their guidance I would like to know how they proceed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext: One of the purposes of this present protocol is to bring about something in the nature of a code under which the court will hereafter proceed. I presume the court of International Justice at the Hague follows the general practice of any court dealing with international affairs, and makes use of existing international law which in its opinion has a bearing on the question before it.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext: Perhaps the Prime Minister will not mind if I say that a committee has been set up to endeavour to codify certain outstanding views and customs with respect to international law, and when that is done obviously this court will apply such a code to disputes. The reason this court is being set up is because there is no other body in the world able to apply the principles of international law, which are more or less nebulous, to differences between nations.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL PEACE
speechtext: When this code of laws is set up, will each of the nations have to approve of it?

speechtext: That is not quite the question I had in mind, and I am bound to say I intended to look it up, because the Prime Minister cannot be expected to carry all these things in his mind. He will perhaps recall that the United States was unwilling to accept the revised protocol, and informed the nations of the world that they proposed to add reservations. Mr. Root was chairman of a small committee which drafted reservations assumed to be acceptable to the United States, and my memory is that the Senate of the United States has not yet ratified the conclusions at which that committee arrived, as expressed by the reservations.

I think that has been done in several instances, but just where we stand with respect to it now I am not quite sure. I am not quite in order; I am only speaking with the permission of the house, but I fancy we all agree that it is highly desirable that the American republic should be a party to this protocol. The United States was not a party to the original protocol. The revision to which I have referred was one by which it was hoped the United States would become a party to that protocol.

That is why the present Chief Justice of the United States became a member of that court, and the other day the president nominated a dfistinguished international jurist from Massachusetts to take the place of Chief Justice Hughes on that court. If we give our accession to it now as the

subtopic: ACCESSION OF UNITED STATES TO PERMANENT COURT

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ACCESSION OF UNITED STATES TO PERMANENT COURT
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the protocol relating to the accession of the United States to the protocol of signature of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice, signed at Geneva, in respect of the Dominion of Canada, on the 14th September, 1929, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: In 1923 the President of the United States invited the Senate of that country to approve the adherence of the United States to the statute of the permanent court. No action was taken at that time on the president's recommendation, but in 1926 the Senate approved of the accession of the United States subject to five reservations, which were communicated to the secretary general of the league. A conference of states, parties to the original protocol of December 16, 1920, was held in Geneva in 1926 to consider these reservations and a deadlock developed on the subject of the fifth reservation concerning advisory opinions.
No progress was made for the next two years, but in 1928 the United States took the initiative in requesting, through the intermediary of Mr. Elihu Root, the reopening of the negotiations which had been dormant since 1926. The committee of jurists which at this time was engaged in revising the statute of the permanent court undertook to prepare a draft protocol which would enable the United States to adhere to the court. This protocol was approved by the tenth assembly of the League of Nations on September 14, 1929, and signed on that day for Canada by Senator Dandurand. It was signed by the United States on December 9, 1929, and by fifty-one other powers in the interim.
It is unnecessary to dwell on the great value to international peace and good feeling which must arise from the participation of the United States in the work of the permanent court. The difficulty which stood for so long in the path of its accession has been successfully surmounted in the protocol now before the house.

speechtext:
My understanding is
that parliamentary approval, where it is necessary, is in some countries awaiting the action of the United States, but that in many instances parliamentary approval is not necessary and executive action is all that is required. I am only speaking from memory, because I did not take the trouble to look up the matter in my books. As it stands at the moment we were bound to adopt the first resolution, but with respect to the one now before the house I rather fear that if the Senate of the United States does not approve of it our ratification will be nugatory, because it would have to go back to the main body for reconsideration, it being really a contract between the powers. I had the benefit of listening to a very instructive address upon the subject by Hon. Newton D. Baker, who was a member of the administration of the United States at one time, and hence I have followed this question with a great deal of interest. The pressure in the United States to have the Senate approve of the protocol has been and is very considerable; whether or not it has been successful I cannot say.
So far as the motion is concerned certainly I desire to agree in every way with what has been said and done, but whether or not it may be nugatory, in consequence of the fact that the necessary action has not been taken by the United States, I cannot say. However, it will do no harm in any event; if it becomes necessary to do it over again all the other nations will be in the same position.

No atonement can be made for the punishment which these young men have undergone if they should be proven to be innocent. Unless there is very grave doubt as to the guilt of the three young men, something should be done to relieve Messrs Lacasse and Fontaine, as, according to the statement of the other three, their punishment would appear to be unjustifiable.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WAR VETERANS' ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this bill is read the third time it would be well, I think to have removed any possible misunderstanding which may exist to the effect that the passing of this bill will conclude the work of the committee which has been dealing with returned soldiers' problems. As the house is aware, this bill came from the committee with its unanimous recommendation of support and has passed second reading without controversial discussion. When the committee on returned soldiers' problems was appointed, it was stated that it would be given the widest latitude in dealing with returned soldiers' problems, that is to say, the widest powers and authority. The committee has already devoted much time and energy to the task laid upon it. I am advised that at the present time the committee has before it proposals involving a complete change in the organization and machinery dealing with the awarding of pensions. Three proposals are being studied and it is hoped that within a very short time there will be presented to parliament for its consideration a recommendation for putting into effect an entirely new system for the presentation, hearing and awarding of pensions. In addition, the associated veteran bodies have made suggestions which cover major amendments proposed to be made to the Pension Act. Amendments are being considered to the Soldiers' Settlement Act and the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act. I have thought it advisable to make clear to the house that in asking that this measure be given its third reading the government is not merely proposing to shelve the further work which the committee was expected to carry out at the time it was appointed. The intention is quite the opposite, namely, to further the work of the committee and enable it to be completed at the earliest possible moment. To assume that the committee would permit itself to be used for the purpose of retarding or shelving legislation in the interest of the returned men is 
entirely unwarranted, and any such assumption should be resented by members of the house and the committee. The government proposes to grant every facility for the passage of legislation based upon the committee's recommendations.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the view taken by this side of the house has been that when a matter of this character arises it should be submitted to a select committee of this house. We are fortunate in having a large number of returned men on this side of the house, and they constituted largely the committee which considered the measure introduced by the Minister of Pensions (Mr. King). Where an unanimous conclusion has been arrived at as to the character of the legislation which should be enacted to meet new conditions, then we are only too delighted to see that conclusion reflected in the unanimous support of the house. So far as it is possible, every effort has been made to prevent matters of this kind becoming contentious in the sense of their being considered from a partisan point of view. I have had occasion to complain, and I suppose I will continue to have occasion to complain, of the introduction of politics into matters of this kind. The evidence is sometimes very striking, and sometimes most offensive to those of us who have no control over expenditures, but this committee having arrived at an unanimous conclusion, so far as those who sit to your immediate left are concerned, we are very pleased indeed to be able to support this legislation.
I am very glad the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has mentioned the Pension Act. It will be recalled that during the course of the discussion which took place in this chamber there did not seem to be the same desire on the part of the minister to overhaul the whole machinery of the Pension Act, as has now been indicated by the Prime Minister, or as was indicated by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. King) after the long discussion which took place upon the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Muskoka-On-tario (Mr. McGibbon) on the second reading of the bill. The announcement that this committee will be continued for the purpose of considering and arriving at conclusions as to how the machinery for the granting of pensions can be impoved will, I am sure, be received with great satisfaction throughout the country. The complaints are really such that I think they will yield to very simple treatment and in that regard I know there is a well defined view amongst many men that at

Toronto Terminals Railway
the moment a few short sections would probably cure the main difficulties that have been indicated in the administration of the act.
As regards soldier settlement matters, the action taken the other day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), in accordance with the recommendations of the Audit Board, in making a further appropriation of 810,000,000 as against loans outstanding to the settlement board, is a step in the right direction so far as it goes, but it will be difficult to salvage much of the personal property and the committee dealing with the matter will find a great deal of difficulty in arriving at a satisfactory conclusion as to how that situation should be dealt with. subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting the Canadian National Railway Company to provide for the issue of new securities by the company, guaranteed by the Dominion, not exceeding $8,609,000, the aggregate face value of the original securities, to repay temporary loans negotiated by the company as successors by amalgamation to the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada for the purpose of retiring the five per cent ten-year refunding mortgage gold bonds of the Central Vermont Railway Company, dated May 1, 1920, amounting to $8,609,000.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext:
Here is something very
serious-the placing of a guarantee of this country behind securities for a railroad in the United States of America. I certainly think it is a wrong policy. I understood that in the reorganization of the Central Vermont railway its securities were to be financed without our guarantee. If you put the guarantee of the Canadian National Railways behind those securities, that is one thing; if you put this country behind them, it is another. It amounts to the same thing in one sense, but not in another. The whole of the Central Vermont system is in the United States, and I am sure the hon. minister will remember the discussion about the Minnesota and Manitoba railways. A small mileage of that railroad is in the state of Minnesota, and some grave constitutional difficulties arose in connection with freight rates and matters of that kind because of that fact. That was many years ago.
Now, does the minister think as a matter of public policy that the Dominion of Canada should guarantee the bonds of a railway in another country? I confess to him that I have thought about it a great deal and have been unable to find any evidence of any other country ever having done so. Surely if the road is as valuable as it is thought to be since
the reorganization, the securities should be sold the same as other railways sell their securities -in the United States; and if not, we should finally, after very careful consideration, determine what our future course is to be as a matter of policy and act upon it. We have the port of Portland on our hands now, and we have this and one or two other railways in the United States in our possession. Some very thoughtful writers, I observe, are of the opinion that we should sell our United States' holdings. I suppose the hon. minister saw the article some time ago in this connection suggesting that that be done. I fancy I reflect the mind of a very great many Canadians who are very, very apprehensive when you ask this Dominion to put its guarantee behind the securities of a railway in a foreign country. I should like the minister's explanation of the matter in the light of that fear that has been expressed to me in letters that I have received since the resolution came on the order paper. Certainly, I repeat, my understanding was that the Canadian National Railways and the Central Vermont railway were arranging the finances, and that the Dominion of Canada as such would not appear in the matter.

The hon. minister has it wrong, I am sorry to say. If he will look at his resolution he will see that the first part of his statement is correct, but not the latter part. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure respecting the Canadian National Railway Company to provide for the issue of new securities by the company-
That is, by the Canadian National Railways.

guaranteed by the Dominion, not exceeding $8,609,000, the aggregate face value of the original securities, to repay temporary loans negotiated by the company as successors by amalgamation to the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada for the purpose of-

Of what?
-for the purpose of retiring the five per cent ten-year refunding mortgage gold bonds of the Central Vermont Railway Company, dated May 1, 1920, amounting to $8,609,000.
The Central Vermont railway issued ten-year gold bonds at five per cent for $8,609,000 in 1920; they are now coming due. The Central Vermont railway should meet them because they are their obligation. We have reorganized the Central Vermont railway through receivership, and we now control its capital stock and the issue of its securities, which I understood were sold without the guarantee of the Dominion. My information was given to me by one of the officials, without having his books before him, that the road is operating now on a profitable basis. I do not say it is earning sufficient to pay interest on all its securities, but it is making a little money and is now a first rate road. The Governor Smith family that at one time, as the hon. minister knows, controlled the Central Vermont railway, have now, by process of receivership, been eliminated from control, and the capital stock belongs to us, but it cost many millions of dollars to reorganize it through the receivership. These $8,609,000 ten-year gold bonds mature this year. I think there is some other money in there too than the Central Vermont railway bonds. It strikes me that the Central Vermont railway should arrange its own finances.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext:
It might have been better before answering my hon. friend's question if I had given the background connected with this matter. Many years ago the old Grand Trunk Railway of Canada became associated with the Central Vermont Railway system. As time went on the relationship developed to the point where the Grand Trunk railway secured control of the Central Vermont railway. This road was in receivership back thirty-one years ago, and in the reorganization which then took place certain financial assistance was given by the Grand Trunk railway, for which it received seventy-three per cent of the common stock of the Central Vermont system. In 1920 the Central Vermont railway had some $12,500,000 of securities maturing which it found very difficult to finance, and the board of directors of the Grand Trunk railway at that time placed the guarantee of the Grand Trunk railway behind the securities of the Central Vermont railway both as to principal and interest. In 1920, as many hon. members know, there were disastrous floods in the state of Vermont, with the result that bridges were destroyed, grades washed out and other serious damage done to the system. It was necessary 
of course to make good this damage. The Central Vermont railway was then thrown into a receivership and, as my hon. friend stated a moment ago, that receivership terminated a short time ago by the Canadian National railway system, who were the inheritors of the old Grand Trunk railway, securing complete control of the stocks of the Central Vermont system.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: Just there, to enable the minister to go on with his statement without further interruption, that was the time, it occurs to me, that a thoughtful administration would pause and consider whether or not they should let somebody else take over the Central Vermont system instead of ourselves. In other words, might not the first loss have been the best loss?

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext:
Of course, my hon. friend
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) was then in charge of the railway department. I think the judgment of the government at the time was that the position taken by the Canadian National Railways management was sound. In other words, they had either to look after these maturities or let the whole thing go by the board. Not only did the Canadian National railway system, as the inheritors of the old Grand Trunk railway, have a very substantial financial interest in the Central Vermont railway, but the Central Vermont railway was also of very great value to the Canadian National system as part of its transportation organization.
When the company was thrown into the receivership in 1927 following these disastrous floods there were still outstanding $8,609,000 of these bonds which had been issued in 1920 and which had been carried by the Grand Trunk Railway. Of course they immediately became due, and to protect them the Canadian National Railways through a process of temporary financing found the funds to take them up. It remained in that state until the receivership was finally discharged in the month of January of the present year. The present measure simply seeks to enable the Canadian National railway system to issue these securities with the guarantee of the government. They are securities of a general kind which would be guaranteed by the government to repay the temporary financing. I believe that was done through the Canadian banks in 1927, when $8,609,000 worth of bonds were required to be taken up.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: Were they repaid?

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: The bonds were taken up and were repaid, as I understand it; that is why the temporary financing was done.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: They were not due until May 1st of this year.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: They became due through the receivership.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: A receivership does not make a bond due.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: I am told that that is the occasion for having these securities.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext: The Canadian National Railways were responsible for very much more; I think they were responsible for about $38,000,000 altogether. But the special financing of the Canadian National Railways which in the budget of this year the minister reported had been successfully covered by an issue, was the sum of $40,000,000 borrowed from the banks to cover the various outstanding maturities which had been redeemed. The Canadian National
Railways are now the sole holders of the bonds of the Central Vermont system, and it is now necessary to provide for the temporary financing for the purpose of taking up these bonds. The present bill provides for that. Consequently it does not add anything to the obligations of the Canadian National Railways. I am informed that the value of the Central Vermont system to the Canadian National railway system is very considerable indeed. The Central Vermont system repre-
C.N.R.-Loan

sents the distributing end of the New England states, largely for the heavy traffic on the Grand Trunk western lines in that part of the United States lying west of the province of Ontario. The traffic originating on the Grand Trunk western lines hauled through the province of Ontario and Quebec, is passed on for distribution in the New England states through the Central Vermont system. This traffic is perhaps the most valuable under the control of the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext:
I am afraid the minister has not grasped the significance of the questions which were asked. There was a receivership; why were these bonds not cleaned up in the receivership? As a general rule when a company goes into the receiver's hands it does so for the reason that it cannot pay its debts. In this case a receiver was appointed; ultimately the property was sold under the hammer and this country through the Canadian National Railways, bought it in. The question I ask is how did this country buy it in unless it was bought in subject to the payment of $8,500,000 of bonds or subject to some other provisions of which we have no knowledge. I suppose those provisions will be stated and the matter will be cleared up before the special committee. If the Canadian National Railways took up these bonds in order to buy the property it means that we are putting $8,500,000 into property because we bought it at a receiver's sale. We otherwise would not have it at all, but having bought the property we have to pay the prior encumbrances registered against it. That is the whole story as I see it. If it was a receiver's sale and it was sold subject to $8,500,000 in bonds, we have to pay them off. From the remarks of the minister I gathered that the bonds were retired by temporary loans and before title could be completed in court. They had to get money so that the bondholders could be paid off and they paid them in order to get title to the Central Vermont Railway. My point is that this parliament should have been consulted as to whether or not we should have bought in that property. That is the difficulty I am in. I will admit that the railway is very valuable for the purposes of distribution, but there is no other company capable of operating it. No one else could take a lease for ninety-nine years, or whatever it might be. We have put enormous sums of money, perhaps $25,000,000 or $30,000,000, into this property since the receivership. Apparently what has happened is that the Canadian National Railways, at a receiver's sale, bought this property which was subject to a Central Vermont mortgage 
loan of eight and a half million dollars, and having bought the property we had to pay off that amount by temporary borrowings to enable a title to be made by the referee or judge in equity. The receiver went out of possession and we issued Central Vermont securities. It seems to me that if Central Vermont securities were issued they should have been placed in the treasury of the Canadian National Railways as against any contributions we might make, but the question I put to the minister for his consideration is whether the guarantee given in connection with any railroad which is out of the country should not be the guarantee of the railway company-the Canadian National Railways-instead of the guarantee of the Dominion. There is not very much difference in fact but there is a great difference in law. The one involves the nation and the other a corporation; the one involves the Dominion of Canada and the other the Canadian National Railways, which is an entity. With the information supplied by the minister I believe we now understand the situation; that is, this property was sold subject to an obligation, which obligation was paid by the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR READJUSTMENT OF PENSIONS

speechtext:
Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
. That it is expedient to provide for the readjustment in accordance with the terms of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act of the pensions of officers and constables of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were retired to pension prior to 31st May, 1924, and who were in receipt of extra pay during the whole or part of the period from 15th May, 1919, to 30th May, 1924; and to readjust the pensions of widows of officers who had received the extra pay as aforesaid.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR READJUSTMENT OF PENSIONS
speechtext:
This resolution is for
the purpose of introducing a bill to give effect to demands which have been made and recommended by various members of the house, among whom is my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). Under the statute of 1919, the governor in council was authorized to pay a bonus or extra pay to the officers of the mounted police. This bonus was paid for five years, the order in council being extended from year to year until 1924. In 1924, this extra pay was consolidated with the regular or statutory pay, and since that date the pay received by the men has included the bonus paid during those five years. At the same time the rate of pension was increased in order to be based upon the new salaries including that extra pay, but only from 1924. The few officers who were retired during the period extending between 1919 and 1924, and who were being paid this extra bonus when their retirement took place, were not included and they were not granted this new rate of pension to which they would have been entitled had the consolidation taken place earlier. They were receiving this additional salary, but it was not included in the pension which was granted to them. All the associations of the old mounted police officers have been asking the govern-

Judges Act Amendment
ment to include those few men in order that they might be granted the same pension. I may say that they are very few and unfortunately they are rapidly disappearing. At. the present time the extra amount which will be added to the pension bill will be only about $8,000 and this amount will decrease gradually as those men disappear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR READJUSTMENT OF PENSIONS

I pressed upon him the claims of a certain number of pensioners of the old police force, who because of the change in pay by reason of the discontinuance of the bonus, found themselves receiving a much smaller pension than those who left the force a little later with the same number of years to their credit, the fact being that what was a bonus was converted into salary and naturally it being so converted, the pension was based upon the salary they were receiving. In this way men with a lesser number of years of service found themselves in some instances receiving a somewhat larger pension than those who had taken pension in previous years. I should like to learn from the minister the number of persons affected, and another question pressed upon me by those interested is whether or not it will be applicable to widows of pensioners.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Judges Act to provide that an annuity equal to his salary at the time he ceased or ceases to hold office may be granted to a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada or of the Exchequer Court of Canada who held office on 31st March, 1927, and continued or continues in office until he attained or attains 75 years of age; and that an annuity equal to two-thirds of the salary annexed to the office which such judge holds at the time he so ceases to be a judge may be granted to a judge of the said courts, appointed after 31st March, 1927, attaining 75 years of age after service of 10 years, or aggregate service of 10 years in that office and as judge of a provincial superior court.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee; Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the members of the committee will no doubt remember, in 1927 the Judges Act was amended so that judges of the Supreme Court of Canada and the Exchequer Court of Canada-it applies not to other courts but merely to the federal high court-on reaching the age of seventy-five should cease to hold office. It was provided in that act that on retirement the judges of these courts would be granted a pension or annuity equal to two-thirds of their salary. At that time the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George raised the point that with respect to judges who had been appointed prior to the enactment of this new law it was not fair to deprive them at the age of seventy-five of part of their salary; that they had been appointed for life and that the least we could do, if it was desired to provide for their com-
Judges Act Amendment

pulsory retirement, was to respect what my hon. friend then called a contract or agreement and to give them an allowance equal to their full salary. I did not agree with my hon. friend at the time, but I must say that since I have been reconsidering the matter I have found that there is much force in that contention; and for those judges who were then members of the court, and they are very few indeed, this law will provide an annuity equal to their salary. Of course all judges appointed following this legislation will take office with the full knowledge that their term will expire when they reach the age of seventy-five, and they will be granted a pension amounting only to two-thirds of their salary.
I presume that the case of Mr. Justice Mignault is covered by this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I congratulate the minister upon doing him this justice, though it is tardy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is right.

The only point I wish to
make is this. As I said before, there are judges who have reached the age of seventy-five who are still competent to carry on judicial work, and it might be well for the Minister of Justice to consider whether their services should not be made available in case of the temporary absence of other ju'dges from the court, or made available for such work as is given to judges upon commissions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As far as acting on
commissions is concerned, there is nothing to prevent judges who have reached the age of seventydive and are fit to do the work from being engaged for special work of that character.

Their services, it seems to
*me, should be made available without salary.

On the second reading
of the bill I was going to refer a little more [DOT]at length than my hon. friend from St. Law-rence-St. George has done to that very matter. Why should we not provide that judges might sit ad hoc?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You mean retired
judges?

Yes. In England, Lord
Mersey used to go down and hear divorce cases when there was a full list, although he was a man of eighty. Frequently that has been done in England. Now that we are providing for pensions for judges, I think we

might provide that if any retired judge is willing to sit he might be called in to sit ad hoc for the purpose of making a quorum or ensuring a full court. The real difficulty with the judges of seventy-five has been the strain of continuous work, but their vast experience would certainly be very useful if it could be utilized on special occasions. During the summer I had occasion to think of another matter, and I made up my mind to speak to the minister in that sense. I had not intended to do it just now, but my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George has brought it back to my mind. I think that if we pay a pension with respect to all tne retired judges we should have a call on their services to sit aid hoc in any appeal court if it is thought desirable to have them. I do not know whether it can be entirely worked out or not, but m Great Britain it has worked very satisfactorily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The suggestion is certainly worthy of consideration, and I promise my hon. friend to look into the matter.

I notice that in England, as the leader of the opposition says, judges who are practically retired do sit not only in probate and admiralty but in other divisions from time to time in order to fill vacancies ad hoc. I know men who have reached upwards of eighty years who perform such functions.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Lapointe thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 133, to amend the Judges Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 126, respecting the Department of Marine.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext:
On Friday I gave all the particulars, I think, which the house would wish to have with respect to this bill and the next two on the order paper. The purpose of these measures is simply to divide what is at the present time the Department

Department oj Marine
of Marine and Fisheries into two separate departments, a Department of Marine and a Department of Fisheries. The law officers of the crown thought that it was best to proceed by creating the two new departments, and then formally to repeal the old act under which the Department of Marine and Fisheries exists to-day. This bill, as well as the_ bill respecting the Department of Fisheries, is to all intents and purposes, in its phraseology and provisions, identical with the Marine and Fisheries Act as it now stands, only such changes being made as are essential to separate the two departments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext: I understand that it is proposed to put dredging in the hands of the marine department?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext: For a long time it has appeared to the government that some reorganization of the work of some of the departments would be in the public interest and it has seemed advisable to have dredging brought as largely as possible into the Department of Marine instead of having it retained, as it is now, in part in the Department of Public Works, in part in the Department of Railways and Canals, and in part also in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The idea is to get as far as may appear to be desirable all the dredging into the one department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext: If there is one matter in Canada about which it might be said that scandals have arisen, it is dredging.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext: This ought to prevent it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER
speechtext:
This will add to it because it is putting the dredging into the department where it does not belong. The Public Works department should handle it because it has the facilities. I had to read a year ago last spring a judgment given by the judge of the exchequer court in connection with a dredging contract which was awarded by one department and dealt with by another. The Public Works department has the engineers, it has the machinery, to take care of this work. That is its business. I learned at that time that the Department of Railways and Canals, for instance, also has engineers who are capable of dealing with certain phases of dredging contracts. The marine department up to the present moment has not been equipped particularly for that business; the Public Works department and the Railways and Canals department have been. When I read the testimony in that case where the applicant was awarded a large sum of money, I am bound to say I
felt the crown should have taken an appeal from the decision of the exchequer court. A dredging contract had been made, it had been assigned, and then boulders larger than those expected were found. In the end the exchequer court gave judgment for a substantial sum of money. At the time I discussed the subject of dredging with some of our friends, and I think if the Prime Minister will make inquiries he will find that two of the departments are peculiarly equipped at the present moment both as to dredges and staff to deal with it. The very words "railways and canals" involve an engineering staff with the requisite knowledge to deal with the situation. The marine department originally was never intended to deal with these matters; when Mr. Smith was deputy minister, it was not a department dealing with matters other than those touching shipwrecks, shipping and fisheries. Now that a special commission has recommended a separate department of fisheries, Professor Macmillan is not going to be a tremendously busy man if he gets the position. He will have a few weeks work, I suppose, before a general election, but in any event it does not appear to me that there will be such a tremendous amount of work in the fisheries department alone as to keep the new minister very busy. My friend from Quebec would seem to think that the fishing was good. He might make it an all the year round job, but I doubt even that. But, seriously, I do think that if the Prime Minister will look into this, he will see that the public works and railways and canals departments have an adequate engineering staff and already own a considerable quantity of dredging equipment.
I should like the Prime Minister to look into the cost of dredging in the various departments as shown by the Auditor General's report last year. It is one of the most amazingly interesting studies in the world. I have not the time these days to go into it that I had in the days gone by, but if my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) will for a moment lay off fruits and vegetables and devote himself to ascertaining just how much it costs to dredge channels one summer and then redredge them next spring he will realize what a profitable avocation dredging has become. It is really one of the most highly paid callings that I know of, the pearl diver has nothing on dredging now. In days gone by the pearl divers used to bring up very valuable pearls from the sea bottom, but their gains are as nothing compared with the profits of modern dredging in Canada. There is my friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Sinclair)-if he will look into it a little now that New Zealand
Department oj Marine

butter has been taken care of to his satisfaction, he will find that dredging is really a most profitable enterprise. I suggest to the Prime Minister that before he turns over dredging entirely to the marine department he study the matter from the economic standpoint, especially in view of the experiences in connection with the new harbour in Hudson bay. There is a dredge up there on top of a wharf that they are finding it difficult to use, as the hon. minister told us last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATE DEPARTMENT PRESIDED OVER BY A MINISTER

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to discuss a topic which I have discussed at various times in the past, that a railway outlet to the Pacific coast should be provided from the Peace River country.
I do not think there is universal agreement as to the state of prosperity of Canada as a nation, but I believe it is generally agreed that there is at least an easing off in employment as compared with a year ago. One of the major contributions in the past to the prosperity of Canada has been the construction of railways and other similar undertakings. During the past four or five years large expenditures have been made in the construction of the Hudson Bay railway and the Welland canal. Both these undertakings are nearing completion and I believe it necessary that similar large scale developments should be carried on in order to provide for at least an equal number of workmen to that engaged upon these two large undertakings.
I desire at this time to emphasize the advantage to Canada of the development of new districts, such as the Peace River country. There is no question but that during the period of the rapid development and settlement of the three western provinces there was a very rapid growth in industries in eastern Canada. It is some time since it was first realized in Canada that the rapid settlement of the west had a direct relation to the prosperity of the industries of the east. I have in my mind the report of the royal commission on the transfer of the natural resources of Manitoba, and the following is to be found at page 35:
Now, dealing first with free homesteads, it must be remembered that a rapid increase of population throws upon a provincial government a heavy burden of expenditure for education, road-building, the administration of justice, etc. It is wrong, we think, to assume, as we have been asked to assume, that, if the public lands of Manitoba had been handed over to the administration of the provincial government, the government would have adopted a free homestead policy similar to that of the Dominion. On the contrary, we find all along, from what was said by exponents of the Dominion policy in 1870 and down to the creation of Alberta and Saskatchewan in 1905, that the assumption entertained was that Manitoba, and later the new provinces, if given the control of their lands, would use them, not for free homesteads, but for the purpose of revenue. It was feared from the very beginning that Manitoba, if allowed the control of its lands, would adopt a policy of settlement by land sales, which would necessarily prove to be slow, and would thus defeat the desire of the Dominion to bring about rapid settlement for the general benefit of Canada.
Before private members' day was taken away, I had on the order paper a motion in connection with this question of the Peace River outlet. I stated in that motion that I believed it was a matter of national necessity. I believe it is so because of the argu-
1784	COMMONS
Peace River Railway-Mr. Kennedy
ment contained in the paragraph I have read from the report of the royal commission on the transfer of the natural resources of Manitoba. I believe in the general interests of the whole Dominon we require a rapid, reasonable and sound development of the Peace River country.
Not so very long ago we were discussing agriculture in the west generally, and I think it was the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) who referred to the fact that one of the causes of unemployment was the coming of the combine, and other large-scale machinery in the farms of western Canada. We all know that the two difficult, slow operations in western farming are ploughing and taking care of the harvest. The small tractor has apparently solved to a large extent the ploughing problem. The coming of the combine has solved the harvesting problem. There has, however, been a tremendous displacement of labour on the farms of the older settled areas of the three western provinces. That is one reason why, without such a large immigration into Canada from abroad during the last few years, we have had a large new settlement in the Peace River country. In 192S and 1929 more than 5,000 new homesteads were taken up in the Grande Prairie and Peace river districts. The homesteads taken up represented an area of 1,760,000 acres and if certain purchases of Hudson's Bay land be added, because some settlers who came in bought land from the Hudson's Bay Company, the area taken up is still larger. The settlers who came in are not the ordinary "suitcase" homesteaders. There is a steady stream of settlers' effects, such as horses, farm tractors and general farm machinery, moving back from the railway stations to points convenient to the new homestead areas. Perhaps more important than the fact that the settlers have equipment is the fact that a large percentage of them have had experience in the very type of farming they are going to undertake in the new settlements of the Peace River country. Undoubtedly the new homesteads taken up in the Peace River country during the last two years have made a tremendous difference in Alberta, Saskatchewan and even Manitoba as well as to some extent British Columbia, in relieving what would otherwise have been a much more acute unemployment problem than we had during last winter.
I believe the outlet should be built as soon as humanly possible. It was two years ago I used the word "forthwith" in my motion,

and the then Minister of Railways objected very strenuously to the word " forthwith " because he said it meant " right away quick." Surely we cannot be in too great a hurry to suit even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar),to use the words that were used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the city of Edmonton in 1924 when he said, regarding the Peace River outlet and the Hudson Bay Railway, that they were an absolute necessity and would be built as soon as humanly possible. But in the light of the treatment that the problem has received at the hands of the government, I am not using the words in quite the sense in which they were used in 1924 and I hope that " as soon as humanly possible " means at least that the government, if it undertakes to accept my motion, as I think it ought to do, will proceed with the construction of the Peace River outlet as rapidly and vigorously as it has done with the construction of the Hudson Bay railway during the last four or five years. That would have been a generally satisfactory application, and I believe it might be even yet, of the words " as soon as humanly possible." I am in just as great a hurry today as I was two years ago, but I believe the matter can be reasonably dealt with by the government and it will be thoroughly justified in going ahead with the Peace River outlet.
It may be asked why I come to parliament with a motion of this kind in view of the purchase of the Edmonton and Dunvegan Railway by the two great railways. I think I ought to read this statement of the Prime Minister again, because it is so definite. I have quoted it a number of times. I even wrote the Prime Minister, giving him a copy of the statement, and on no occasion did he undertake to say that it was not in accordance with what he has said in Edmonton in 1924. This is taken from the Edmonton Bulletin of November 11, 1924:
Premier promises outlet to Pacific Just as soon as humanly possible.
Railway will be built, declares Prime Minister, at mass meeting here.
Government has but minority in Commons; says times are now difficult and everybody must have a little patience, but Liberal party is not falling down on any of its pledges.
"It is the policy of the government of which I have the honour to be the head to introduce a vigorous policy of immigration which will people the vast areas of undeveloped country in the great west," declared the Right Hon.
Peace River Railway-Mr. Kennedy

W. L. Mackenzie King, Premier of Canada, when addressing mass meeting of citizens in the First Presbyterian church last night.
There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development. The Peace River country is amongst the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an absolute necessity. I pledge myself that as soon as it is humanly possible the great Peace River country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied and will open up the country for prospective settlers. I must, however, sound the same note to you here as I did to the citizens of Saskatoon. The times that we are passing through are very difficult, and I would ask you to have a little patience and in as short a time as possible a railway outlet will be provided for Peace river and northern Alberta districts that will open up an era of prosperity for that country which will not be equalled by any other province in Canada.
In those words the Prime Minister of Canada, the leader of the House of Commons, in 1924, accepted the responsibility that he would see that an outlet to the Peace River country to assist the pioneers of that district would be built as soon as possible.
The development of the Peace River country has been interrupted and discouraged over a period of years by its great distance from centres of population, and consequent higher cost of implements of production and necessaries of life, high mileage rates on freight moving in and out of the country, long hauls to and from the railway and high rates and great mileage to contend with in the sale of its products. The indications are that with the larger acreage and with the promise at least of sufficient moisture we shall produce this year one of the best crops we have had in the history of the country; but I realize, of course, that a whole lot may happen to a crop between now and harvest time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The last offer for the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway was that made in June, 1928, by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Previously the Alberta government had offered the Alberta railways, including the Edmonton, Dun-vegan and British Columbia and Canada Central railways, for something like 816,000,000. The Minister of Railways turned down that offer, but the great crop of 1927 came along; the Canadian Pacific directors went through the Peace River country and, upon their return to Edmonton, offered the Alberta government the price which that government had set upon those railway lines.
Complaint has been made that from 1925 to 1928 the Alberta government kept raising the price for these railways, but the reason is quite obvious. Anyone with a business that has been losing money and which has not been able to pay the cost of operation for a few years, and who, within say three years, gets it on a basis where it pays nearly all the fixed charges as well as the cost of operation, naturally would raise the price. That is the reason why the Canadian Pacific Railway Company offered $25,000,000, the price set by the government of Alberta, and no doubt that is the reason why the Canadian National Railways took a fifty per cent interest. For the life of me I cannot understand the wisdom of the policy of the government, when you consider the main line *'f the Canadian National Railways west from Edmonton and lack of local traffic. If it was a good proposition to take a fifty per cent interest in the northern Alberta railways and get half the traffic for the Canadian National railways, I do not see why it would not have been a good policy to take over the whole thing and get all the traffic. I never 
could see any justification for that policy from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railways or of the Dominion government. We all know that the Canadian National Railways want business more than anything else, and in my judgment by refusing to take over the northern Alberta railways they lost one of the best chances any railway ever had to get main line traffic. The responsibility for this action must rest on the government and the management of the Canadian National Railways.
Now I wish to come to the question of branch lines. Every time this matter has been debated here and in committee the Minister of Railways and the presidents of the two railway systems would always say, "We need Peace River branch lines, and after we get branch lines we will build an outlet when the traffic justifies it." There is something in that, but I should like to point out that three years ago we were from 150 to 200 miles behind with the branch line program and to-day we are at least 500 or 600 miles behind. I submit -that the people who have left the older portions of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta and gone into the Peace River country on their own initiative, people who are not asking for any special help like those who are in the ranks of the unemployed to-day, have the right to expect the Dominion government to see that they will get railway facilities just as soon as it is humanly possible to do so.
Consider the Battle River district, where there has been a development much more rapid than anything we have seen in the Peace River district. That district has been settled during the last three years, and to-day there is a highway, only four feet narrower than the standard highway throughout the western provinces, running from the railway into the Battle River country. We have at least 2,000,000 acres of settled land fit for the plough in the Peace River country and not one-half of it is under the plough yet, without taking into consideration the 1,700,000 acres taken up during the last couple of years. I am quite satisfied that it is absolutely unjust, so far as the railways and the government are concerned, to say that the question of an outlet for that country will not be dealt with until the branch line situation has been remedied.
It just means that the 20,000 pioneers who went into the Peace River country, who developed it and demonstrated to the railways and the Dominion of Canada that it was a real asset, are going to be asked to carry the burden of expensive freight rates as long as they live. We say that these people are entitled to and should have the shorter mileage

Peace River Railway-Mr. Ladner
and lower rates which they would get through an outlet to the Pacific coast. If we were catching up with our branch line program; if we were getting to the point where fewer settlers were 80, 90, 100 and even 200 miles from the railway there might be some justification for that argument, but when we are getting further behind with our branch lines I submit that the argument is absolutely valueless and falls to the ground. It may be all right for the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways; they are getting from 6 cents to 10 cents extra for hauling grain out of the Peace River country to Fort William and Port Arthur and to Vancouver and Prince Rupert. I submit, however, that it is not fair for the government to say to the pioneers, "We are going to ask you to carry that burden just so long as we are behind with our branch line program."
I think I have said enough on this question, Mr. Speaker. I have tried to show that we are going ahead rapidly with the development of the Peace River country. The Prime Minister made a promise in 1924, and he has fallen down on that promise. I think that opinion is general, and I do not see how he could expect the settlers to think otherwise. In spite of that, however, there is no disposition to sulk or sit down and do nothing. The development in the Peace River country has done a great deal to offset what otherwise would have been a much more serious unemployment trouble during the last few years. In that country there are 10,000,000 acres of land just as good as the 600,000 acres which produced 16,000,000 bushels of grain in 1929. In comparison with our policy in connection with the Hudson Bay railway and other railway problems, I submit, as the Prime Minister has said, that it is crying out for action, and I would like to see the government take definite steps to deal with the matter.
I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Spencer:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"immediate steps be taken to implement the pledge of the Prime Minister given at Edmonton in November, 1924, with regard to the Peace River outlet."

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question is one of vast importance to the province of British Columbia and the Peace River district, and for that reason I intend to occupy the time of the house for a few moments with some observations regarding this amendment. The last speaker (Mr. Kennedy) has referred to the promise made in 1924 by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister visited the province of
British Columbia in November, of 1929, and I would like to call to his attention the report of a speech he delivered which appears in the Daily Province under date of November 16, 1929. Out of two hours discussion and oratory which the leader of the government gave to some three thousand people in Vancouver, the newspapers featured the following article:
Peace River Outlet Endorsed as Policy by Prime Minister
Endorsement of the Peace River outlet to the Pacific, was indicated by Premier Mackenzie King to an audience of nearly 3,00(1 which taxed the capacity of the new auditorium on Friday night. For nearly two hours, he reviewed his eight years of administration.
"As a government we believe in the Pacific outlet for the Peace," said the Premier, "and we don't intend to allow the railways to dillydally in reaching their decision. If they do, then the authority of the state can be called on to make them reach one."
The Premier reiterated his assurance given at Edmonton that "the spearhead of immigration as far as his government's policy is concerned, will be the Peace river."
It is to be noted that some changes now are taking place with respect to the Department of Immigration. The report continues:
The Liberal government, the Premier added, has implemented its promises in completing thr Hudson Bay railway, and everywhere on the coast he has heard "Peace River outlet to the Pacific."
"I ask you, is this government, which has dealt with these great transportation problems brought about reduced freight rates, organized scattered national lines, constructed a great railway from central. Canada to the Atlantic -cannot this government be trusted to find an outlet from the centre of the Dominion to the Pacific?"
Those are the words he uttered to three thousand people in the city of Vancouver. But he went farther than that. Knowing the susceptibility of the people of the west with regard to the promises of his government, and the knowledge of the shadow of a doubt which they sometimes cast upon his utterances just prior to an election, the Prime Minister forestalled that situation with these words:
"I am told that the people don't want any promises. Well, I won't make any promises -you know what trouble we had in the Senate with our branch line bills."
I ask the house to consider what was said in that pledge. Did he or did he not make a promise when he said, "As a government we believe in the Pacific outlet for the Peace, and we don't intend to allow the railways to dilly-dally in reaching their decision. If they do, then the authority of the state can be called upon to make them reach one"? Is that a commitment of government policy, ox

Peace River Railway-Mr. Ladner
is it not? Is that a principle to which the government is committed, and which the people may expect to be carried out, or is there an uncertainty in vague expressions which will enable the Prime Minister to escape? Towards the end he made an attempt at escaping when he said, "You know what trouble we had in the Senate with our branch lines bills."
This is a matter which should be beyond the pale of party politics. A vast area of some
74,000,000 acres is awaiting development and immigration, and now stands ready for the hand of constructive statesmanship. In glowing terms and with the fervour credited to great speakers, the Prime Minister in 1924 told the people of western Canada in the plain language of plain people: If you elect us to power, we will see to it that this railway is constructed. Six years have passed and the settlers are forced to go in of their own volition. The government's immigration policy is a farce, the spearhead of immigration pointing south, and the minister is to be prorogated, so to speak. Six years pass by, and another election approaches, so the right hon. gentleman appears upon the platform in Vancouver and expresses himself in a wholesome way by saying: If you entrust me once more with power, I will see to it that the railway systems will not dilly-dally; if they do, I will bring the authority of the state to bear upon the heads of those business men who have failed in their duty so far as transportation from the Peace River district is concerned.
The merits and desirability of an outlet from the Peace River district, and an aggressive policy to settle that district, are beyond argument. The facts have been placed frequently before the house, and the undertakings of the government are specific. Their obligations are well founded and well bounded. An undertaking was made six years ago which they have purposely and deliberately failed to carry out, and yet the Prime Minister went to Vancouver in November last and reiterated in more vigorous terms the same pledge and the same undertaking. I ask the Prime Minister: Will he this evening, in reply to this amendment which is simply a request that he fulfil the honour of his undertaking, pledge to the people of this country the immediate fulfilment of his promise with regard to the construction of the Peace River outlet?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise to support most cordially the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) regarding an immediate outlet for

this great inland empire. The fame of the Peace River country has gone out not merely to the whole of Canada but to the whole world, and its further development must and will contribute greatly to Canadian prosperity. I would like the house to realize the full significance of the words which I have thought out, because I would not at this moment endeavour to give a false impression regarding the greatness of the country for which we are advocating a direct outlet to the Pacific coast. An era of vast expansion is awaiting this great territory as soon as the proper transportation facilities are provided. This plea has been made continuously in this house since 1924, and I think it is but right and proper that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the members of the government should be faced squarely with the problem which confronts them. I want to be impartial and enable the Prime Minister to explain exactly why for six years the government has failed to listen to the views which have been presented to this house. It is up to the government at this important time when the problem has in a way been taken out of the government's hands and made the subject matter of public opinion, as I shall show in a few moments.
Let me give the house a few excerpts in regard to this important question, the Peace River outlet. I find that in 1924, before the parliament of Canada, the Prime Minister considered that this question was of paramount importance, To prove that, I will quote his words delivered in the city of Edmonton in the presence of the very people who were advocating what we have been advocating for the last six years. It is said that a man who possesses the gift of words and disguises his thoughts by sophistication, is not doing what an educated man should do, and I am going to give to the Prime Minister exactly what I believe he meant when he uttered these words in the city of Edmonton on the 12th October, 1924. He said:
The future prosperity of this country is bound up in the development of its great natural resources, and, to develop these resources it is necessary to have a large increase in population. There is to the north of this city a great tract of land that is crying out for development. The Peace river country is amongst the richest in Canada, but before the proper development of that country can take place an outlet to the Pacific coast is an "absolute necessity." I pledge myself that as soon as it is humanly possible the great Peace river country will be given that measure of railway relief that will bring to the pioneers of that country the outlet they have been so long denied and will open up the country fu prospective settlers.

Who said that?

Peace River Railway-Mr. Brady

speechtext:
The Prime Minister of Canada uttered these significant words in 1924. For six long years the people of the Peace River country and the people of British Columbia, who depend upon those great natural resources have been waiting for the implementing of the words of, at that time, the greatest and most important man in Canada.
Let me go a little further and speak about some other ministers of that day. I refer to the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), at that time Minister of Railways. As reported on page 2212 of Hansard of 1927, the then Minister of Railways had this to say:
"Mr Dunning:	Only a relatively limited
number of the farmers are now a long distance from existing lines of transportation, and the problem is really one of providing a more economical way to the markets of the world.
Then he said that in order to assist in the development and settlement of the Peace River country and to encourage immigrants, the problem is one of providing a more economical outlet to the people already there and within a reasonable distance of the existing lines of railway.
What does the acting Minister of Immigration say? And I am glad to see the minister in his place, because I know he will stand up and say just what he said in 1927. Unfortunately, however, actions speak louder than words. I would have been delighted to see that before to-day he had urged the final solution of the great problem of the Peace River country:
Hon. Charles Stewart:	I am a strong
advocate of the outlet to the coast and 1 support the suggestion that there be a survey made with a view to having the route definitely settled, this year if possible.
Thus we find three important _ cabinet members of the government realizing the importance of solving the problem of this great inland empire. If I am to judge tonight of what they have done I must bring in a verdict of disapprobation of their lack of vision and understanding regarding not merely Peace River and British Columbia but Canada as a whole. What a wonderful chance was given to the present government and the Canadian National to solve this problem. The Canadian Pacific, understanding the potentialities of that great country, of its own accord took up the solution of this problem and bought from the Alberta government the railway lines, at what price? At the very price dictated by the Alberta government. What is the inference to be drawn from that? It means that the Canadian Pacific realized the importance of controlling the wonderful wealth of that great territory.
How far have we proceeded towards getting an outlet from the Peace River to the Pacific by the amalgamation of the two great transcontinental railways? I should like to know.
I doubt very much whether the agreement entered into between these two great transcontinental railways is going to solve the problem wihch it was within the power of the present parliament of Canada to settle on its own initiative. What has happened since the agreement between these two great transcontinental railways was made? In September 1929, the Canadian chamber of commerce, representing not merely the whole of Canada, but also the British Empire, England, Scotland and Wales, paid a visit to the Peace River country because of the wonderful stories they had about it's wealth and fertility. Who were the members of the Canadian chambers of commerce who went to the Peace River country in 1929? Whom did they represent and what was the result of their visit to that country? I will briefly mention who were the men and women who comprised the Empire chambers of commerce who visited the Peace River country. It was the largest, the most influential and most representative body of business men and women within the empire. Why did they go in there? Why did they choose in 1929 to spend a week, nay, ten days visiting the Peace River country? The answer is this. Already the fame of that country had gone abroad. What was the result of their visit? I am going to add to the words of the Prime Minister in 1924, of the Minister of Railways and Canals and of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization in 1927, the words of the president of the Canadian chamber of commerce on his return to Calgary from the Peace River country. If I used these words myself I would probably be looked upon as exaggerating, but Mr. Birks, of Montreal, the president of the Canadian chamber of commerce, after visiting the Peace River country from Spirit river to Grande Prairie, to Dawson Creek, Rolla, Beaverlodge, Peace River, and back to Calgary, asked what he thought of the Peace River country, replied:
"We were amazed and thunderstruck at the immensity and wonderful fertility of this great Peace river country."
He was amazed; he was thunderstruck. What did S. P. Gundy, of Toronto, say on his return from that visit? If there is one practical man who could not be carried away by emotion I think it is this very gentleman; and here are his words:
"Never in our lives have we met such people, or enjoyed a trip like this. Wherever I go

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one who is familiar with the question brought up by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) will deny that it is one of very considerable importance and interest to the people of that vast district. The settlement of the Peace River area during the past four or five years has been stimulated, and I think there is every reason to expect that the progress thus far made will continue, perhaps not in the same degree or at the same rate, but certainly at a rate comparable with what has happened in the older districts.
While I cannot quite agree with all the arguments that my hon. friend has advanced in support of his resolution, nevertheless I can

Peace River Railway-Mr. Crerar
say to him at once that some of them are deserving of the best consideration of the house. With the background of what he has said I, of course, personally am not familiar, not having been in the house during recent years when the discussions that he has referred to took place. All I can do in any remarks that I may make is to deal with the situation as I have ascertained it since I came into the department a few months ago.
As my hon. friend stated, there have been several investigations as to possible outlets to the Pacific coast. That work I understand, so far as the railway companies are concerned, is not yet completed.
