speechtext: Does the Prime Minister still stand by that statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Most decidedly I still stand by it. Let me read further from the text of the article:
The Premier reiterated his assurance given at Edmonton that "the spearhead of immigration as far as his government's policy is concerned, will be the Peace River."
Continuing, the first minister reviewed the activities of the two great railways in making a survey,-
This is the part my hon. friends did not read.
*-at his request, of the construction problems associated with the outlet, and added they were working together on branch line development in the Peace River area. Parliament, he felt sure, will want to know what these railway companies think about the matter before taking any action. Until they finish their surveys, it will be difficult to get the house to act. '
My hon. friends did not read that part of the speech, and in deliberately omitting it they were seeking to put both myself and the government in an entirely false light. What I said at Vancouver I adhere to at the present time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon. friend will please keep his seat. I did not interrupt him, and I have very little time in which to finish my remarks. If he so desires I shall be just as pleased to move the adjournment of the debate and conclude another day. What I had in mind, as I expressed it here, was that parliament would wish to know-and in speaking of parliament I refer not only to this House of Commons but also to the other chamber through which all measures have also to pass-before it either granted charters to the companies or made the necessary appropriations for a railway of the character described, what the railway companies themselves thought about it. I submit that if the government attempted to bring forward a project for a railway from the Peace River country to the Pacific ocean or to connect at any given point or points with other lines which run to the Pacific; without having in its possession the views of the two railway companies and their reports upon the surveys which they had made, it would be very difficult if not impossible to get the necessary support to pass the legislation through parliament.
Happily, in more particulars than one, we as a government, are in a different position to-day from the position we have been in during previous years in our dealings with many matters in parliament. We can with some degree of certainty, when we bring forward a measure which we know to bo

Privilege-Mr. Kennedy
supported by necessary information and essential consideration, undertake to say that in all probability the purpose of the measure will be implemented in its course through both houses. I want to repeat here what I said at Vancouver: We have asked each of the railway companies to expedite the surveys which they are making. I have spoken personally to Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; I have spoken personally to Sir Henry Thornton, president of the Canadian National Railways. The present Minister of Railways and Canals said to-night that he also has expressed the views and desires of the government to the presidents of these two systems, and the former Minister of Railways and Canals, the present Minister of Finance, made a similar statement. We all have impressed upon the presidents of these systems that it is the desire of the government to have this matter expedited and the surveys completed, that it is our view that at an early date agreement should be arrived at by the two companies as to the route which they will jointly recommend, and that failing agreement by them the government itself will undertake to make a decision.
Since it is eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I will move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, May 6, 1930.
